reason: Attacked hardest on punctuation, and it holds. The modern text disagrees with the proposal, which is why this looked breakable: the Gutenberg Jane Eyre (#1260), downloaded and read, prints "I am no bird; and no net ensnares me; I am a free human being with an independent will, which I now exert to leave you", a semicolon where the proposal has a colon and a comma where it has a semicolon. So I went to the named edition. I downloaded the Internet Archive scan the verifier cites and checked its metadata first: title "Jane Eyre : an autobiography", volume "v.2 c.1", publisher "London : Smith, Elder, and Co.", date 1847, creator Bronte, Charlotte. It is the named first edition, not a reprint. Its text reads "I am no bird; and no net ensnares me: I am a free human being with an independent will; which I now exert to leave you." The proposal is the first edition exactly, marks included, and the verifier's restoration of the full sentence through "which I now exert to leave you" is correct; the truncated form with a full stop after "independent will" is the quotation-site invention. The locator is right by count: the passage falls between the headings for chapter VIII and chapter IX in that volume, and volume II chapter I opens "I both wished and feared to see Mr. Rochester on the day which followed this sleepless night", which is chapter 16, so volume II chapter VIII is chapter 23. Scene and speaker check out: it answers Rochester's "Jane, be still; don't struggle so, like a wild, frantic bird that is rending its own plumage in its desperation" and is followed by "Another effort set me at liberty", the orchard at Thornfield, Jane speaking for herself. Bronte is not banned, not on the misattribution list, stands at one of three (month 2), and shipped.js returns no shipped or near match. In scope, publishable, tag Fiction is the form of the work, source line 112 characters, name first, no dash, curly quotes only. One fair criticism that does not reach the line: the note says the comparison texts close the second clause with a comma where the first edition sets a semicolon, but it does not mention that they also set a semicolon where the first edition sets a colon after "ensnares me". The note is incomplete about the modern texts, not wrong about the shipped wording.
